rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatihah has several names and is called the Seven Oft-Repeated because it recurs in the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: also called Fatihat al-Kitab ("The Opening of the Divine Writ"), Umm al-Kitab

rows.speaker: Bukhari
rows.claim: Bukhari reports that the Prophet named it Umm al-Kitab because it condenses the Qur'an's fundamental principles.
rows.anchor: According to Bukhari, the designation Umm al-Kitab was given to it by the Prophet himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah condenses divine oneness, creation and grace, accountability, guidance, prophetic continuity, righteous action, afterlife, and worship of God alone.
rows.anchor: it contains, in a condensed form, all the f undamental principles laid down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its prayer form invites constant repetition and reflection by believers.
rows.anchor: this surah has been formulated as a prayer, to be constantly repeated and reflected upon

rows.speaker: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib
rows.claim: Some authorities, including Ali, considered Al-Fatihah the first revelation.
rows.anchor: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib) were even of the opinion that it was the very first revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authentic reports in Bukhari and Muslim show that the first five verses of surah 96 began revelation, contradicting Ali's view.
rows.anchor: th is view is contradicted by authentic Traditions quoted by both Bukhari and Muslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatihah was probably the first complete surah revealed at once, explaining Ali's view that it was first.
rows.anchor: the first surah revealed to the Prophet in its entirety at one time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most authorities count the opening invocation as verse 1 of Al-Fatihah; in other surahs it precedes the text without being counted.
rows.anchor: According to most of the authorities, this invocation (which occurs at the beginning of every surah

rows.speaker: Ibn al-Qayyim
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes rahman as God's inherent, inseparable abounding grace and rahim as that grace manifested in creation.
rows.anchor: the one advanced by Ibn al-Qayyim (as quoted in Manar I,48)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Worlds” covers every category of physical and spiritual existence.
rows.anchor: the term "worlds" denotes all categories of existence both in the physical and the spiritual sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb combines rightful possession and authority with rearing, sustaining, and fostering something from its beginning to completion.
rows.anchor: It comprises the ideas of having a just claim to the possession of anything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the definite article, rabb is used in the Qur'an exclusively for God, sole sustainer of all creation and ultimate authority.
rows.anchor: the designation rabb is applied, in the Qur'an, exclusively to God as the sole fosterer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed are those given prophetic guidance and enabled to benefit from it.
rows.anchor: by vouchsafing to them prophetic guidance and enabling them to avail themselves thereof

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nearly all commentators equate God's condemnation with the harmful consequences people incur by knowingly rejecting guidance and disobeying its commands.
rows.anchor: According to almost all the commentators, God's "condemnation" (ghadab, lit., "wrath") is synonymous

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari reads the final two descriptions as qualifying the blessed people: they were not condemned and did not go astray.
rows.anchor: Some commentators (e.g., Zamakhshari) interpret this passage as follows

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Baghawi and Ibn Kathir reject Zamakhshari's qualification reading and take the final phrases as distinct groups on a wrong course, as Asad does.
rows.anchor: Other commentators (e.g., Baghawi and Ibn Kathir) do not subscribe to this interpretation

rows.speaker: Al-Ghazali and Muhammad 'Abduh
rows.claim: They distinguish informed rejection of a recognized message from straying when truth never arrived or arrived too corrupted to recognize.
rows.anchor: Al-Ghazali or, in recent times, Muhammad 'Abduh) held the view that the people described

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation includes inner coherence and qualities fitted to an entity's intended function, adapting it in advance to its conditions of existence.
rows.anchor: He endows it with inner coherence and with qualities consistent with the functions which it is meant to perform

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links God's determining and guiding to the closing sentence of 25:2 and to 20:50.
rows.anchor: Cf. the last sentence of 25:2 and the corresponding note 3; also 20:50

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The herbage's decay is a metonym for God's bringing life and dealing death.
rows.anchor: metonymically, "who brings forth life and deals death"

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators take the passage as addressed to Muhammad and promise that he will remember the Qur'an except what God wills him to forget.
rows.anchor: The classical commentators assume that the above words are addressed specifically to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the commentators' strained explanations of why God might make His messenger forget revealed Qur'an, especially the appeal to abrogation.
rows.anchor: many unconvincing explanations have been advanced from very early times down to our own days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the address to Muhammad as also directed to humanity generally, linking it to the opening revelation in 96:1–5, especially the teaching of knowledge in 96:3–5.
rows.anchor: the above passage, though ostensibly addressed to the Prophet, is directed at man in general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes cumulative empirical and rational knowledge transmitted across generations and civilizations; God lets humanity acquire and share it, while obsolete learning may be forgotten as experience expands.
rows.anchor: mankind's cumulative acquisition of empirical and rational knowledge, handed down from generation to generation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Observation and speculation remain valuable but limited and cannot alone disclose ultimate truths.
rows.anchor: all knowledge arrived at through our observation of the external world and through speculation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghayb is what lies beyond human perception; because human knowledge is always incomplete, people need revelation to find their way through life.
rows.anchor: all that is intrinsically beyond the reach of human perception (al-ghayb)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The easy way means ease of mind and peace of spirit.
rows.anchor: towards an ease of the mind and peace of the spirit

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Razi
rows.claim: Baghawi and one alternative interpretation by Razi take the command as a reminder regardless of whether it seems useful.
rows.anchor: Thus Baghawi, as well as Razi in one of his alternative interpretations of this phrase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned person's inability to die or live follows from having kept away from divine reminders, as in 74:28–29.
rows.anchor: in consequence of having remained aloof from the divine reminder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and Moses exemplify earlier revelations, underscoring continuity in religious experience and the shared basic truths of all prophets.
rows.anchor: These two names are given here only as examples of earlier prophetic revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suhuf literally means leaves or scrolls and is synonymous with kitab, so Asad renders it as revelations.
rows.anchor: The noun suhuf (sing. sahifah), which literally denotes "leaves [of a book]" or "scrolls"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was probably revealed around the middle of the Meccan period and takes its title from al-ghashiyah in its opening verse.
rows.anchor: from the participial noun al-ghashiyah in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Overshadowing Event is the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: I.e., the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: Al-Qiffal
rows.claim: Al-Qiffal takes hell's food and drink as a metonym for utter hopelessness and abasement.
rows.anchor: According to Al-Qiffal (as quoted by Razi), this kind of hellish drink and food

rows.speaker: Jawhari
rows.claim: Jawhari says dari' is a bitter, thorny plant when dry and connects its root to becoming abject or abased.
rows.anchor: which is said to be a bitter, thorny plant in its dried state (Jawhari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders dari' metaphorically as the bitterness of dry thorns, and treats the boiling spring similarly, recalling Qur'anic hamim.
rows.anchor: hence my rendering of this (obviously metaphorical) expression as "the bitterness of dry thorns"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: They explain the singular spring generically, meaning many springs.
rows.anchor: as Zamakhshari and lbn Kathir point out, the singular form has here a generic import

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spring symbolizes life-giving water, like the rivers often used in Qur'anic depictions of paradise.
rows.anchor: This metaphor of the life-giving element is analogous to that of the "running waters"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the raised thrones, Asad refers readers to his note 34 on 15:47.
rows.anchor: See note 34 on 15:47

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denying resurrection makes the idea of a conscious Creator meaningless, which motivates Asad's interpretive insertion about those who deny resurrection.
rows.anchor: a denial of resurrection and life in the hereafter renders the concept of a conscious Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibil usually means camels, a generic plural without a singular form.
rows.anchor: it denotes, as a rule, "camels": a generic plural which has no singular form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers the lexically attested meaning of rain-bearing clouds: it keeps the Qur'anic appeal universal across eras and settings, while camels would narrow it to the Prophet's Arabian contemporaries.
rows.anchor: it also signifies "clouds bearing rain-water" (Lisan al-'Arab, Qamus, Taj al-'Arus)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clouds reading also fits the surrounding sky, mountains, and earth by evoking evaporation, rising vapour, condensation, and rainfall.
rows.anchor: such an allusion to the miraculous, cyclic process of the evaporation of water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal phrase means that the Prophet has no power over them.
rows.anchor: Lit., "thou hast no power over them"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daybreak symbolizes spiritual awakening; the ten nights allude to Ramadan's last third in 13 BH, when Muhammad received revelation and could awaken humanity spiritually.
rows.anchor: the "ten nights" is an allusion to the last third of the month of Ramadan

rows.speaker: Baghawi
rows.claim: On Sa'id ibn al-Khudri's authority, Baghawi and one alternative reading by Tabari take even and odd as creation's multiplicity against the Creator's oneness.
rows.anchor: Baghawi, on the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Khudri, as well as Tabari

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evenness implies counterparts and relations among things, matching the polarity described by azwaj in 36:36; al-watr or al-witr means the single One, God, without comparison or likeness.
rows.anchor: The concept of the "even number" implies the existence of more than one of the same kind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies Iram as the legendary capital of 'Ad, now buried under the sands of Al-Ahqaf.
rows.anchor: Iram, mentioned in the next verse, seems to have been the name of their legendary capital

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The valley is Wadi al-Qura, north of Medina on the old caravan route from South Arabia to Syria; Asad points to notes on 7:56 and 7:59.
rows.anchor: The "valley" referred to in the sequence is the Wadi 'l-Qura, situated north of Medina

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of Pharaoh's epithet, Asad directs readers to his note 17 on surah 38.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of this epithet, see surah 38, note 17

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari, Razi, Baydawi
rows.claim: They read the contrast introduced by fa-amma as connecting back to the evidence for truth in verse 5: people usually focus on this world's immediate gains rather than the hereafter.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari, Razi, Baydawi

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says the person treats God's bounty as something owed to him.
rows.anchor: he regards God's bounty as something due to him (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person treats reduced means as divine injustice rather than a trial, which may lead to denying God's existence.
rows.anchor: not as a trial, but as an evidence of divine "injustice"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means people feel no urge to feed the needy, paralleling 107:3.
rows.anchor: I.e., "you feel no urge to feed the needy"

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Although the wording literally says God's Sustainer comes, most classical commentators understand it as the disclosure of transcendental majesty and the manifestation of judgment.
rows.anchor: almost all of the classical commentators understand as the revelation (in the abstract sense of this word)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his note on 73:12–13 for this expression.
rows.anchor: See note 7 on 73:12-13

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators take balad as a city, identify “this city” as Mecca, and read “thou” as Muhammad; Asad says this is plausible given Qur'anic emphasis on Mecca's sacredness.
rows.anchor: The classical commentators give to the term balad the connotation of "city"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers the broader reading: balad means humanity's land, Earth, and “thou” addresses humanity; the oath invokes its earthly environment.
rows.anchor: the sequence - as well as the tenor of the whole surah - seems to warrant a wider

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari convincingly reads the begetter and offspring as every parent and all descendants, humanity from beginning to end.
rows.anchor: According to Tabari's convincing explanation, this phrase signifies "every parent and all their offspring"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine al-walid includes mothers as well as fathers.
rows.anchor: The masculine form al-walid denotes, of course, both male and female parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boast implies inexhaustible resources and possibilities; as “man” means humanity, it represents the decadence-era belief that human ambition has no limits and worldly interests alone define right and wrong.
rows.anchor: his resources - and, therefore, his possibilities - are inexhaustible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks whether a person thinks he is answerable to no one but himself.
rows.anchor: Does he think that he is responsible to none but himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tongue and lips enable a person to recognize and voice God's existence or at least ask for guidance.
rows.anchor: to recognize and to voice the truth of God's existence or, at least to ask for guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Companions of the right side” literally means people on the right side; see 74:39.
rows.anchor: Lit., "people (ashab) of the right side"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The left-side people are those lost in evil; the phrase evokes afterlife fires of despair rising over sinners' hearts and enclosing them, as in 104:6–8.
rows.anchor: the fires of despair in the life to come "rising over the [sinners') hearts"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's builder signifies the qualities producing harmony and coherence in the visible cosmos; the earth's spreading signifies the qualities behind its beauty and variety.
rows.anchor: the wondrous qualities which are responsible for the harmony and coherence of the visible cosmos

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs here means the whole human self or personality: physical body together with the elusive life essence called soul.
rows.anchor: denotes here the human self or personality as a whole

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawwa here means formed in accordance with an intended pattern, as in its earlier use at 87:2.
rows.anchor: For this particular connotation of the verb sawwa, see note 1 on 87:2

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interwoven bodily, emotional, and intellectual elements of human personality follow organically from contemplating the universe's grandeur as evidence of God's creative power.
rows.anchor: the implied allusion to the extremely complex phenomenon of a life-entity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans can rise spiritually or sink into immorality; this polarity is essential to human nature and gives right choices value through moral free will.
rows.anchor: it is this inherent polarity of tendencies which gives to every "right" choice a value

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 7:73–79 and its notes for Thamud's story, used here to illustrate humanity's potential wickedness.
rows.anchor: given here as an illustration of man's potential wickedness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The she-camel account is explained in a note on 7:57; the command to let her drink is tied to 26:155.
rows.anchor: For the particular reference to the injunction, "Let her drink", see 26:155

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel legend was already well known in pre-Islamic Arabia.
rows.anchor: The formulation of this passage shows that the legend of the she-camel was well known

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers to his note on 7:91 for his rendering of aqaruha.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of aqaruha, see note 61 on 7:91

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's cruelty to God's creatures shows lack of fear of retribution and therefore lack of real belief in God.
rows.anchor: their total lack of compassion for God's creatures showed that they did not fear His retribution

none: source text is cut off after “i.e., the elements”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human life here and in the hereafter comprises two stages of one continuous entity.
rows.anchor: man's life in this world and in the hereafter are but two stages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says no one has a favor owed to them; with a future orientation it also rules out expecting reward.
rows.anchor: the phrase implies also the expectation of a reward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan reference may recall Muhammad's father's death before his birth and his mother's death when he was six; more broadly, everyone is created and resurrected alone.
rows.anchor: Possibly an allusion to the fact that Muhammad was born a few months after his father's death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sa'il means anyone who asks, including someone seeking help in physical or moral difficulty or seeking enlightenment, not only a beggar.
rows.anchor: which signifies not only a "beggar" but anyone who asks for help

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ellipsis implies speaking of the Lord's blessings rather than of one's suffering.
rows.anchor: Sc., "rather than of thy suffering"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means “thy breast” or “bosom.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "thy breast" or "bosom"

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari, citing Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd, identifies the burden as past sins that have now been forgiven.
rows.anchor: Tabari, on the authority of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Muhammad this apparently refers to mistakes before prophethood and echoes 93:7, where he was found lost and guided.
rows.anchor: this relates apparently to mistakes committed before his call to prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr primarily means reminder or remembrance, secondarily what makes someone remembered with praise, and here figuratively denotes eminence or dignity.
rows.anchor: The primary meaning of the term dhikr is "reminder" or "remembrance"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fig and olive stand for eastern Mediterranean lands, especially Palestine and Syria, where many Qur'anic Abrahamic prophets preached, culminating with Jesus.
rows.anchor: these two species of tree may be taken as metonyms for the religious teachings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinai points to Moses and the law revealed there, which remained valid until Muhammad and was also binding on Jesus in essentials.
rows.anchor: the religious law valid before, and up to, the advent of Muhammad - and in its essentials binding on Jesus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secure land is Mecca, where Muhammad was born and received his call.
rows.anchor: this land secure" signifies undoubtedly (as is evident from 2:126) Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first three verses present the ethical unity of the genuine teachings of monotheism through Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: the fundamental ethical unity underlying the teachings - the genuine teachings - of all the three historic phases

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads din as the moral law set out in verses 1–3 and also taught across monotheistic religions; denying it rejects human moral choice and God's justice, although the law should be self-evident.
rows.anchor: to the validity of the moral law - which, to my mind, is the meaning of the term din

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authorities agree that 96:1–5 began Qur'anic revelation in Ramadan's last third, thirteen years before the Hijrah; the exact date is uncertain and Muhammad was forty.
rows.anchor: all authorities agree in that these five verses were revealed in the last third of the month of Ramadan

rows.speaker: Bukhari
rows.claim: Bukhari reports Muhammad's retreat to the cave of Hira for long vigils and prayers before the angel's visit.
rows.anchor: "solitude became dear unto him, and he used to withdraw into seclusion in a cave of Mount Hira

rows.speaker: Bukhari
rows.claim: In the report of the first encounter, the angel repeatedly commands “Read”; Muhammad says he cannot, is pressed three times, then understands he must receive and understand God's message.
rows.anchor: the angel "seized me and pressed me to himself until all strength went out of me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report appears in Bukhari's introductory chapter, with nearly identical versions in Bukhari elsewhere and in Muslim, Nasa'i, and Tirmidhi; verses 6–19 came later.
rows.anchor: identical versions of this Tradition are found in two other places in Bukhari as well as in Muslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqra may mean read or recite; Asad prefers read because it denotes conscious reception aimed at understanding, whereas reciting can merely deliver memorized or written words aloud.
rows.anchor: the former rendering is, to my mind, by far the preferable in this context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense creation verb indicates that divine creation is continually repeated.
rows.anchor: the act of divine creation (khalq) has been and is being continuously repeated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fertilized ovum origin contrasts biological simplicity with intellectual and spiritual potential, pointing to conscious design and purpose in life.
rows.anchor: contrasting the primitiveness and simplicity of his biological origins with his intellectual and spiritual potential

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pen symbolizes writing and recorded knowledge, clarifying the summons to read; writing carries ideas and experience across people, generations, and cultures, making human knowledge cumulative and giving each person access to what they could not know alone.
rows.anchor: "The pen" is used here as a symbol for the art of writing or

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's teaching also means revelation through prophets of spiritual truths and moral standards that human experience and reasoning alone cannot establish unequivocally.
rows.anchor: God's "teaching" man signifies also the act of His revealing, through the prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ar-ruj'a means both that everyone returns to God for judgment and that all existence returns to God as its source.
rows.anchor: everyone will inescapably be brought before God for judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–8 reject human self-sufficiency and tie every moral distinction between right and wrong to responsibility before a supreme power; without that responsibility, morality loses meaning.
rows.anchor: all moral concepts - that is, all discrimination between good and evil, or right and wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording suggests an attempt to prevent prayer; classical commentators identify Abu Jahl's efforts to stop Muhammad and followers praying publicly at the Ka'bah, in a passage revealed at least a year after 96:1–5.
rows.anchor: most of the classical commentators see in this passage (which was revealed at least a year later than the first five verses)

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: They read the passage historically as referring to Abu Jahl's attempts to stop Muhammad and his followers praying at the Ka'bah.
rows.anchor: an allusion to Abu Jahl, the Prophet's bitterest opponent in Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the passage applies beyond that incident to all efforts to exclude religion from shaping social life, whether by privatizing it or dismissing the need for metaphysical guidance.
rows.anchor: the purport of the above passage goes far beyond any historical incident or situation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwa is rendered throughout as God-consciousness; this is the earliest occurrence in revelation, and Asad interprets the opponent's invocation of religion as plainly not intended to deepen others' God-consciousness.
rows.anchor: the obvious implication being that this is not his aim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person turns from the truth because arrogance prevents him from facing it.
rows.anchor: because in his arrogance he cannot face it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dragging someone by the forelock is an old Arabian expression for utter subjection and humiliation; Razi reads forelock metonymically as the forehead where it grows.
rows.anchor: an ancient Arabian expression denoting aa person's utter subjection and humiliation

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says nasiyah, “forelock,” is metonymic for the forehead on which it grows.
rows.anchor: as Razi points out, the term "forelock" (nasiyah) is here used metonymically

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Commentators with a historical reading take “his council” as Mecca's pagan elders' council, dar al-nadwah.
rows.anchor: the traditional council of elders (dar an- nadwah) in pagan Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad more probably reads the council as the arrogance that makes people imagine themselves self-sufficient, recalling verses 6–7.
rows.anchor: more probably, I think, it is an allusion to the arrogance which so often deludes man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening refers to the revelation of 96:1–5 and the beginning of Muhammad's mission, placing Al-Qadr in the early Meccan period.
rows.anchor: a reference to the revelation of the first five verses of the preceding surah
